questions.q: What does Ferriss say you should focus your working time on?
a: The few tasks that produce the biggest results
The tasks you can finish the fastest
The work that keeps you busiest
The projects others expect from you
questions.why: Lesson 1 urges effectiveness over efficiency, spent on the 20 percent that yields most.

questions.q: What does the 80/20 rule mean in this summary?
a: A small share of effort produces most of the results
Most people work at only 20 percent capacity
You should work 80 hours and rest 20
Eighty percent of projects should be outsourced
questions.why: Lesson 1 applies the Pareto principle to time, and notes the split is often even more lopsided.

questions.q: How should you validate a business idea?
a: Ask people to pay before you build it
Survey friends about whether they like it
Build a prototype and then test demand
Research what competitors are charging
questions.why: Lesson 2 says to get money first, since pre-selling reveals demand before you invest.

questions.q: Why does Ferriss recommend charging a premium?
a: You need fewer customers and they are less hassle
It makes your product seem scarce
It lets you skip customer service entirely
It attracts buyers who like to bargain
questions.why: Lesson 3 shows that higher prices mean fewer sales needed and calmer, easier clients.

questions.q: What kind of buyer does a premium price tend to attract?
a: Low-hassle buyers who complain and return less
Buyers who demand the most support
Buyers who compare every price closely
Buyers who purchase only once
questions.why: Lesson 3 says such customers do not have to think twice about every cent they spend.
